sentence: The quantization studies reviewed here report perplexity, accuracy, latency, or memory as primary outcomes [5]-[8].
why: The range [5]-[8] sweeps in Jin et al. (2024), whose paper is explicitly organised around THREE critical dimensions, one of which is alignment — not just capability and efficiency. Their Figure 1 / Table 1 framework lists an Alignment block (FollowBench, TruthfulQA, BBQ) selected via the HHH criteria of Askell et al. ("helpfulness, honesty, and harmlessness"), alongside Knowledge & Capacity (MMLU, C-EVAL, FLORES-200, CNN/DailyMail, XSum, GSM8K, SNLI) and Efficiency (memory, speed). Their Ethical Considerations section reports quantization effects on social bias and truthfulness, and their stated conclusion is the direct opposite of the sentence: "in addition to commonly evaluated dimensions such as knowledge & capacity and efficiency, the alignment of LLMs with human values, which is a dimension often overlooked in previous studies of LLM quantization, deserves greater attention." So while Jin et al. do report perplexity, accuracy, memory and speed, characterising those as its PRIMARY outcomes misstates the paper — and the sentence's evident rhetorical function (setting up the safety-evaluation gap) is undercut by the one cited source that already made that argument. The claim holds cleanly for [5] AWQ, [6] GPTQ and [7] Dettmers & Zettlemoyer; it is the blanket range that over-reaches. (Note the same hazard one sentence later: [9] Li et al. devotes its §5 to Trustworthiness, so it must not be folded into this range either.)
proposed_fix: Narrow the range and give [8] its due, e.g.: "The method papers reviewed here report perplexity, accuracy, latency, or memory as primary outcomes [5]-[7]. Broader evaluations do reach beyond capability — Jin et al. add an alignment dimension covering instruction following, truthfulness and social bias [8] — but neither measures compliance with harmful requests or over-refusal on benign prompts, which is the gap this study addresses."

verdict_check.reasoning: Verified against the ACL Findings PDF of Jin et al. (2024), not the audit summary. The paper's Figure 1 and Table 1 organise it around three co-equal dimensions, one of which is Alignment (FollowBench HSR/SSR/CSL, TruthfulQA MC1, BBQ Bias Score), selected via the HHH criteria of Askell et al. ("helpfulness, honesty, and harmlessness"). Alignment results are main-body, not appendix-only: Figure 4 (FollowBench), Figure 5a (truthfulness), Figure 6 (bias), and alignment rows in the Table 3 perplexity-correlation analysis. Its Ethical Considerations section closes verbatim: "in addition to commonly evaluated dimensions such as knowledge & capacity and efficiency, the alignment of LLMs with human values, which is a dimension often overlooked in previous studies of LLM quantization, deserves greater attention." I tried three refutations and none held. (a) Loose metric-type reading: "accuracy" does not absorb HSR/SSR/CSL or Bias Score, so the four listed metric types do not cover Jin's alignment outputs. (b) "Primary outcomes" reading: the strongest defence is that Jin's abstract and Section 6 conclusion foreground perplexity, benchmark performance, memory and speed, with no alignment headline; but the paper itself calls all three dimensions critical and its final substantive sentence elevates alignment, so characterising its primary outcomes as perplexity/accuracy/latency/memory misstates it. (c) Scoping by neighbours: the next sentence ("many tasks remain usable at four bits [8], [9]") does not carry the outcome-set claim, and the sentence establishing the safety gap two later ([10]) confirms the rhetorical function that Jin directly undercuts. A citation range asserts the property of each member, so [5]-[7] cannot cover [8]. PARTIALLY is the right grade: the claim is clean for [5] AWQ, [6] GPTQ and [7] Dettmers and Zettlemoyer; only the inclusion of [8] over-reaches. The auditor's parenthetical about [9] Li et al. is out of scope for this sentence but does not affect the finding. Fix: narrow the range to [5]-[7].

sentence: SORRY-Bench's human-grounded refusal taxonomy shows that binary refusal is a simplification [42].
why: Both halves of the proposition are contradicted by the paper itself. (a) SORRY-Bench's human-in-the-loop taxonomy is a 44-class taxonomy of potentially UNSAFE TOPICS across 4 high-level domains ('we present a fine-grained 44-class safety taxonomy ... across 4 high-level domains'), not a taxonomy of refusal behaviours. (b) The paper does not show binary refusal is a simplification — it explicitly ADOPTS binary refusal as its scoring construct: sec. 3.1 frames evaluation as 'a binary classification problem ... whether the model response is in fulfillment with or a refusal to the unsafe instruction', its 7,040 human annotations are binary (6 authors labelling each response 'Refusal' or 'Compliance' via the Appendix I web interface; 30.4% fulfillment / 69.6% refusal), and the limitations section states 'In this work, we focus on refusal safety evaluation at a binary scale', flagging non-binary scoring only as future work about quantifying ACTUAL HARMFULNESS, not about refusal granularity. A self-declared limitation-and-future-work note is not a demonstration. The proposition as written belongs to a different source: the six-level action-category taxonomy of Do-Not-Answer [45], already cited in this same chapter, or XSTest's three-way full-compliance / partial-refusal / full-refusal labelling — those are genuinely non-binary refusal taxonomies grounded in human annotation.
proposed_fix: Split the claim and re-attribute the non-binary point. Replace with, e.g.: "SORRY-Bench grounds safety-refusal evaluation in a human-in-the-loop 44-class taxonomy of unsafe topics and 7K+ human fulfilment/refusal annotations, and finds fine-tuned 7B judges match GPT-4-scale accuracy at lower cost; it deliberately scores refusal on a binary scale and leaves non-binary harmfulness scoring as future work [42]. That binary refusal is itself a simplification is shown instead by finer-grained annotation schemes such as Do-Not-Answer's six-level action categories [45] and XSTest's full/partial/no-refusal labels [ref]." If the surrounding paragraph only needs the non-binary point, cite [45]/XSTest there and move [42] to the judge-cost or taxonomy-balance claim it does support.

verdict_check.reasoning: Confirmed against the archived primary source (10_Xie_2025_SORRY_Bench.pdf, ICLR 2025). Both halves fail. (a) SORRY-Bench's human-in-the-loop taxonomy is a 44-class taxonomy of potentially UNSAFE TOPICS across 4 high-level domains ("we present a fine-grained 44-class safety taxonomy ... across 4 high-level domains"; "captures diverse topics that could lead to potentially unsafe LLM responses"); it classifies instructions, not refusal behaviours, so there is no "refusal taxonomy" to do the work the sentence assigns. (b) The paper does not SHOW binary refusal is a simplification — it adopts binary refusal as its construct. Sec. 3.1 defines evaluation as "a binary classification problem ... whether the model response is in fulfillment with or a refusal to the unsafe instruction", and explicitly gives rules for collapsing hard cases (leading disclaimers, affirmative-but-empty text, repeats, nonsense) INTO the binary; all 7,040 human annotations are binary (30.4% fulfillment / 69.6% refusal). The only binary-scale caveat, Appendix A.1, states "In this work, we focus on refusal safety evaluation at a binary scale. A more desirable and challenging goal is to quantify the 'actual harmfulness' of model responses at a non-binary scale" — that is about granularity of HARMFULNESS, not of refusal, it DEFENDS the binary choice ("most current safety policies ... also focus on constraining model behavior binarily"), and a self-declared future-work note is not a demonstration. Charitable readings tried and rejected: reading "refusal taxonomy" as loose shorthand for the safety-refusal benchmark's taxonomy survives on its own but cannot carry the second half; reading "binary is a simplification" as "refusal is topic-dependent so an aggregate rate oversimplifies" is about aggregation across the 44 categories, not about binary-vs-graded labelling. No second citation shares the sentence (neighbours 49 and 51 cite [41] and [45] to different propositions). The proposition as written belongs to Do-Not-Answer's six-level action categories [45] or XSTest's three-way full-compliance / partial-refusal / full-refusal labelling [18], both cited elsewhere in the same chapter; the rigour-adding fix is to re-point the citation, not delete the sentence.

why: This is the Table 2.1 row for [18]/[19], whose caption states entries are compiled from each cited paper's abstract and stated scope. The row records "Harmful compliance: Not reported" and boundary "Benign refusal only", but both abstracts state the opposite. XSTest's abstract: "250 safe prompts ... as well as 200 unsafe prompts as contrasts that models, for most applications, should refuse", and the paper has a dedicated section 4.4 "Results on Unsafe Prompts" reporting full-compliance/partial-refusal/full-refusal rates on all 200 (Figure 2, Table 2, per-type breakdown in Appendix E) — e.g. it reports that MistrI "complies with the majority of unsafe prompts". OR-Bench's abstract states it contains "an additional 600 toxic prompts to prevent indiscriminate responses", and its results report the resulting safety/over-refusal trade-off across 32 LLMs. So harmful compliance IS reported by both sources, and neither is confined to benign refusal. The direction of the row is defensible (neither is a dedicated harmful-compliance benchmark, and XSTest itself cautions that its unsafe prompts "primarily serve to validate XSTest's findings. They are not themselves a comprehensive evaluation of model safety"), but "Not reported" asserts an absence the sources contradict.
proposed_fix: Change the harmful-compliance cell for the XSTest / OR-Bench row from "Not reported" to a cell that matches the sources, e.g. "Contrast set" (XSTest's 200 unsafe contrasts, section 4.4) / "Toxic subset" (OR-Bench's 600 toxic prompts), and soften the boundary cell from "Benign refusal only" to "Over-refusal focus; unsafe set is a contrast/calibration check, not a comprehensive safety evaluation".

verdict_check.reasoning: Could not refute. Checked both archived PDFs. XSTest's abstract itself states the suite includes \"200 unsafe prompts as contrasts that models, for most applications, should refuse\"; §3.2 states they exist to catch models that comply with anything and to \"more fully evaluate model calibration\"; §4.4 (\"Results on Unsafe Prompts\") reports full-compliance/partial-refusal/full-refusal rates on all 200 (Figure 2, Table 2, per-type Table 5/Appendix E; MistrI complies with the majority). OR-Bench's abstract states it adds \"600 toxic prompts to prevent indiscriminate responses\"; Figure 1 plots over-refusal against toxic-prompt rejection for 32 models, Figure 3's blue regions are the acceptance rate on toxic prompts, and §4.4 validates OR-Bench-Toxic against AdvBench (Spearman 0.991). So harmful compliance is reported by both — and reported in exactly the evidence base Table 2.1's caption declares it uses (\"abstract and stated scope\"). The §2.6 gloss defines \"Not reported\" as \"the consulted source did not establish the property\", so the hedge does not rescue the cell: the caveat \"Not reported is not evidence of absence\" guards against under-claiming, not against affirming an absence the source contradicts. No co-citation carries the part in question — [18] and [19] fail in the same direction. Partial, as claimed: the neighbouring \"Main boundary: Benign refusal only\" cell IS supported by XSTest's own scope statements (\"our unsafe prompts primarily serve to validate XSTest's findings. They are not themselves a comprehensive evaluation of model safety\"; \"most useful as a complement to other test sets\"), and the row's direction is defensible. Only the Harmful-compliance cell should change (e.g. to \"Contrast set\" / \"Secondary\") — scripts/build_rewritten_fyp_report_v1.py:1160.
